1.e4 c5 2.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation
1.e4 c5 2.c3.background: Named after the Russian master Semyon Alapin (1856–1923), who championed it at the end of the 19th century. For many years it was not held in high regard, since 2...d5 was thought to give Black easy equality; it was revived in the late 1960s by Evgeny Sveshnikov and Evgeny Vasiukov, and Deep Blue played it against Kasparov in the first game of their 1996 match. Today it is considered one of the most solid and respectable Anti-Sicilians.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6.background: Its main line, 2...Nf6 3.e5 Nd5, is the one in current practice against the Alapin and can also arise when Black declines the Smith–Morra Gambit.
1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6.strategy: Hits e4 at once while developing. White usually pushes the pawn to e5 and gains space, but the pawn then becomes a target, and Black's knight lands on an active square where it can be chased with tempo. Black aims to undermine e5 from the flank and the centre; the price is less central space for a time.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 immediately and tries to trade off White's central pawn. Black recaptures with the queen and develops quickly, but the early queen can be hit with tempo by Nc3 once White's c-pawn has been traded off, so Black has to be careful.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 e6.strategy: The most solid reply: it prepares ...d5 and steers towards French Defence structures, with White's extra c3 thrown in. The c8-bishop stays behind its pawns for now. Black gets a sound, familiar structure, but White can still aim for a slight edge.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds pressure on d4, keeping Black's central pawn moves available. It does not prevent 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4, which gives White a two-pawn centre and a slight edge. Sound enough, but a step behind the main replies.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d6.strategy: A sharp try that prepares ...Nf6 against e4. White can take the full centre at once and keep a space advantage, or accept Black's gambit by taking on c5, when Black has given up material for activity.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 g6.strategy: Heads for a kingside fianchetto, the bishop on g7 bearing on d4 from a distance. White answers 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4, and Black has to strike at the broad centre quickly, usually with 4...d5. A viable set-up, but White's extra space makes it harder than the main replies.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 e5.strategy: Stakes out d4 and makes a quick d4 awkward for White, but seriously weakens the d5 square. After 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bc4 White has a solid edge and targets f7 and d5. Playable and rare, yet not recommended.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Qa5.strategy: Pins the c3 pawn along the e1-a5 diagonal once d2 moves, so 3.d4 cxd4 cannot be answered by 4.cxd4. White avoids the issue by developing first and playing d4 later, while the queen on a5 stands exposed. A rare try that is not refuted by force.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 b6.strategy: Prepares a queenside fianchetto with ...Bb7 to pressure e4. It is slow, though: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4 White has a broad centre and quicker development, and Nc3 easily covers e4. A rare, playable try.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out early to watch e5 and the c-file, but does not stop 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4, which gives White a full centre. White's knight then gains time against the queen.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Qb6.strategy: Eyes b2 and, after exchanges on d4, the d4 pawn, but Bc1 covers b2 and 3.d4 cxd4 4.cxd4 builds a full centre. The exposed queen then loses time to attacks by White's knight.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Na6.strategy: The knight aims for c7 to support ...d5 but is badly placed on the rim: 3.Bxa6 bxa6 doubles Black's a-pawns at once, and 3.d4 takes the centre without a fight.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 but does nothing about d4. After 3.d4 the c1-bishop eyes h6, so Black must spend another move on the knight or accept doubled h-pawns after Bxh6 gxh6.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 as in other Sicilian set-ups and loses nothing at once, but it is slow here: it does nothing about White's central break, and Black must still develop and meet the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space but does nothing about 3.d4, and it weakens b5, where a white bishop or knight can settle. Black spends a tempo without developing.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that prevents Bg5 but does nothing about 3.d4 and the centre, and leaves Black a tempo behind in development.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space but loosens g5 and g6 and does nothing about 3.d4. Black spends a tempo without developing a piece or contesting the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside for good: 3.d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against g5, so after 3...cxd4 4.cxd4 Black must spend another move holding the pawn while White has the full centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn for nothing: nothing defends b5, so 3.Bxb5 wins it, and Black has no lead in development or other clear compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 c4.strategy: Overextends the pawn, which nothing defends: 3.Bxc4 takes it at once, and White then has a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 f6.strategy: Weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and takes f6 from the g8-knight: 3.Qh5+ g6 4.Qxc5 wins a pawn, and the king stays exposed.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 f5.strategy: Hangs the pawn, since 3.exf5 wins it at once, and it opens the e8-h5 diagonal against the king without any development in return.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5.strategy: The simplest answer to the threat on e4: with the c-pawn on c3 the knight cannot defend the pawn from there, so White takes first. White gives Black's queen a square on d5, but gets a quiet game in which a broad pawn centre is the aim.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.e5.strategy: Pushes past the pawn and closes the centre, but Black can bring the light-squared bishop out before shutting the pawn chain with ...e6. That gives Black an easier version of the Advance French, so the move equalises for Black and White's e5 pawn becomes a target.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn, but the pawn on c3 already takes the knight's natural square and the d4 break now costs an extra move. Sound and solid, yet Black develops freely and takes the space in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre before e4 is safe, and Black takes the pawn. White regains a pawn on c5, but after the queens come off White has lost castling and trails in development. Playable, but Black is slightly better.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defence
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: The main reply: the queen recaptures and stands safely on d5, since the c3 square is taken by White's own pawn and the knight cannot attack it with a gain of time. Black gets a free development and White the chance to build a pawn centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.background: Lakdawala and Hansen, whose 2022 book is devoted to the line, credit part of its popularity to Magnus Carlsen playing it at the 2022 Chessable Masters. A game with 3...Nf6 is recorded from the 1959 British Championship, where 4.d4 Qxd5 followed.
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Black does not retake at once: the knight develops and the d5 pawn is left attacked by the queen and the knight, so White must decide whether to hold it or give it back. A gambit played for faster development, with real compensation if White defends the pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 e6.strategy: Attacks the advanced pawn with the e-pawn and keeps the queen at home. It is a pawn offer: White can take on e6 and keep the extra pawn, so Black must show that the lead in development is worth it.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4.strategy: Challenges the centre at once and puts the question to the c5 pawn. Black's queen is out early, so White plays for a broad pawn centre and for tempo against it.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: A calm developing move that keeps the d-pawn at home for now. The queen on d5 cannot be driven away by a knight, so White plans the pawn centre with d4 later, but Black gets a move to organise first.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d3.strategy: Opens the c1-bishop and covers c4 and e4, but slows the d4 break that gives the c3 pawn its point. A passive set-up in which Black develops freely and holds the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4, which is now attacked three times by the c-pawn, the knight and the queen and defended twice. White has to support the pawn or resolve the tension, while Black's pieces come out with tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and protects the queen on d5, keeping the pawn structure flexible: Black can still decide later whether to exchange on d4. A natural move that keeps the choice of set-up open.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the centre pawn at once, but it frees the c3 square, from which the b1 knight can attack the queen after White's recapture. A fully playable choice, though it gives White the knight's best square.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to hit d4 from a distance, instead of challenging the pawn or developing a piece at once. Solid enough, but the slowest of the sensible replies, and it leaves White free to develop with the pawn centre intact.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 cxd4 5..strategy: Recaptures with the pawn and keeps a pawn on d4. It reopens c3 for the b1 knight, which can attack the queen, but the pawn on d4 is now isolated, so White trades a long-term weakness for active pieces and space.
Takes the pawn and offers a queen trade. After the trade White has an isolated d-pawn and no attack to hope for, while Black develops easily. Safe but dull, and it gives up the initiative.

Develops instead of recapturing on d4, so White stays a pawn down for a lead in development. Black cannot grab on c3, since that opens the d-file and Qxd5 wins the queen. Sound, but White must prove the activity is worth the pawn.
Develops the knight and adds a second attacker to the isolated d4 pawn. White has to defend it with development, while Black's pieces come out without losing time.
Develops the knight, but ignores the threat of Nc3, which hits the queen at once. Black loses a tempo moving it, and White uses the time to finish its development.

Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and keeps a compact pawn structure, but shuts in the light-squared bishop and ignores Nc3 hitting the queen with a gain of time. Solid but passive, while White develops with the initiative.
Defends the d4 pawn with a developing move and leaves the b1 knight free to come to c3 with a gain of time on the queen. White accepts the isolated pawn and plays for active pieces.
Defends d4 with the bishop and keeps the g1 knight free for later. Sound but slower than developing the knight, and the pawn on d4 stays an isolated target attacked by the queen and the knight.

Hits the queen and leaves d4 defended by the queen alone, so Black can take the pawn. White then plays for development against a king still in the centre. Sound, but White has to prove the compensation, where quiet development keeps d4 safe.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 cxd4 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defence, Central Exchange
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 cxd4 5..strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain with a pin on the knight, which defends d4. Black then piles up on the d4 pawn, and White has to meet that pressure with accurate development.

Strikes at d4 with a pawn, adding a third attacker, and opens lines for Black's pieces. It is the riskier way to fight for the centre: the pawn structure loosens and the queen on d5 can be hit once the d-file opens, so Black has to be sure the activity is worth it.
A natural developing move that walks into 7.Nc3: the queen is hit with tempo, has to retreat, and White's lead in development grows into a large advantage.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 g6 5.Nf.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defence
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 g6 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight and gives the d4 pawn a third defender, so the centre stays together against the pressure of the c-pawn and the queen. White gets a natural developing move for free, since Black has not yet attacked the pawn with a piece.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 g6 5.dx.strategy: Gives up the pawn centre to open the game. The queen recaptures on c5 and Be3 hits it with a gain of time, but the c3 pawn then has no purpose. Easy to play and level, with no plan of a broad centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 g6 5.Be.strategy: Defends d4 with the bishop and keeps the choice of where the g1 knight goes. Sound, but slower than developing the knight, and the pawn on d4 stays attacked by the queen and the c-pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6 5.N.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defence
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Adds a defender to d4 with a developing move, so that the pawn is attacked three times and defended three times. White keeps the pawn centre together and the tension in place.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6 5.d.strategy: Releases the tension in the centre by taking the pawn. Black usually regains it, so White trades its centre pawn for Black's c-pawn and gets an open game, but the isolated-pawn plans are gone. A respected alternative that is easy to play.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6 5.B.strategy: Defends d4 with a developing move and keeps the g1 knight free. Sound but slower than developing the knight, and it leaves the pawn on d4 attacked three times while the queenside pieces stay at home.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nc6 5.N.strategy: Resolves the tension on Black's terms: after White's recapture there is an isolated pawn on d4 that Black's queen and knight can blockade. Black then develops with control of the d5 square and aims at a favourable structure rather than at material.

Pins the f3 knight against the queen, which ties down a defender of d4. Black develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and keeps the tension. It delays the resolution of the centre and gives White time to unpin.
A natural developing move that controls e4 and d5, but it adds nothing to the pressure on d4 and does not yet commit the light-squared bishop. White gets a free move to complete its development.

Recaptures with the pawn, which keeps a pawn on d4 and reopens c3 for the b1 knight. The pawn is isolated, so White trades a lasting weakness for space and active pieces, and has to use its development to keep d4 safe.

Retakes with the knight and invites a knight trade, after which White has to recapture with the c-pawn or the queen anyway and ends up with the same isolated d-pawn, with fewer pieces and Black's queen well placed.
Takes the pawn with the queen, but the knight on c6 takes it: Nxd4, and White gets only a knight back. The queen is lost for a knight and a pawn, so this is a blunder, not a queen trade.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight and gives d4 a third defender against the c-pawn and the queen. White keeps a solid pawn centre and has to meet the development of Black's pieces.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6 5.B.strategy: Develops the bishop and defends d4 while keeping the g1 knight flexible. Sound but slower than developing the knight, and the pawn on d4 stays attacked by the c-pawn and the queen.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Opens the centre by taking the pawn. Black recaptures with the queen, hit by Be3 with tempo, or trades queens and costs White castling; either way the pawn centre is gone and the c3 pawn has little to do.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6 5.N.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Barmen Defence, Modern Line
1.e4 c5 2.c3 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Pins the knight against the queen from outside the pawn chain, which makes d4 harder to defend. Black develops the bishop with tempo and White has to answer the pin carefully.

A solid set-up that guards the d5 square and opens the f8 bishop, accepting that the light-squared bishop is shut in rather than developed. Black aims at the d4 pawn with pieces and a slower, safer game.

Develops and adds a third attacker to d4, keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out. White now chooses how to meet the tension, and the queen on d5 stays exposed to Nc3 once the c-pawns come off.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5.strategy: Meets the attack on e4 by driving the knight away instead of defending the pawn, which the c3 pawn leaves without its natural defender. White gains space and a tempo; the price is an advanced pawn that has to stay supported against Black's pressure.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn instead of pushing it. Solid and safe, but it blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal, gains no space and lets Black develop freely, so White gives up the initiative of the e-pawn push for a quiet game.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once but leaves e4 loose, so Black can take on d4 or on e4. After the capture on d4 White has to push e5 straight away to keep the pawn; the game becomes open and sharp, and Black chooses how to meet it.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5.strategy: The one square that keeps the knight active: it lands in the centre, presses on c3 and blocks the d-pawn's path, so White needs a pawn or a bishop move to challenge it. Black has spent two moves on this knight, so the game is about undermining e5 to justify it.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng8.strategy: Retreats to the starting square. The knight is safe, but Black has moved it twice for nothing while White has gained space and time, so White builds a broad centre while Black starts again.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Ne4.strategy: Walks into a trap: after the quiet d3 the knight has no safe square. Every retreat meets a capture (exf6, exd6 or Bxg5), and the knight can only sell itself for a pawn on c3 or f2.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4.strategy: Builds the broad pawn centre at once and gives e5 a firm support. It threatens c4 to dislodge the knight and then d5 to cramp Black. Black has to strike at the centre immediately, since waiting only lets White's space grow.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards e5 before deciding how to build the centre. It is more flexible but slower than taking the centre at once, so Black gets time to bring pieces against e5 and to organise a counter in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Bc4.strategy: Hits the knight at once, but it retreats with a tempo on the bishop, which a pawn push can chase again. White spends time on the bishop while the advanced pawn has no pawn behind it, and Black equalises without difficulty.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.g3.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto, so that the bishop on g2 will press on d5 and the long diagonal. It is slow: the e5 pawn has no pawn behind it, and Black can calmly build a solid position and undermine the advanced pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Smith-Morra Declined
1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4.strategy: Trades the flank pawn for White's central one, the exchange 1...c5 aims at. White normally recaptures with the c-pawn and keeps a broad centre, which Black then undermines, so the game is about whether e5 and d4 hold.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 d6.strategy: Challenges the advanced pawn at once and frees the c8-bishop. White must decide whether to keep e5 or trade it, and Black gets a solid, flexible game in which the c5 pawn can still strike at d4, at the price of White keeping the extra space.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with a second attacker on d4, beside the c5 pawn, and presses on the e5 pawn, so the centre is tested at once. Black postpones the pawn exchange and keeps the structure flexible.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on e5, the advanced pawn, which only the knight on f3 guards. Black brings a piece into the fight for the centre at once and keeps the pawn structure flexible.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 e6.strategy: Supports the knight on d5 with a pawn and stops the e5 pawn from advancing, so a bishop attack on d5 achieves nothing. Black builds a compact structure and prepares to undermine e5, at the cost of the c8-bishop being shut in behind its own pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 d6.strategy: Attacks the advanced pawn at once and frees the bishop. White can trade on d6 and Black recaptures into an even, simple position, or hold e5 and Black has spent a tempo without gaining space. Sound, but it gives White the easier game.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bc.strategy: Hits the centralised knight and aims along the diagonal at f7 behind it. Black has to decide at once whether to keep the knight or give it up. White chooses piece pressure over a quick pawn centre, and the bishop can later be chased.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Na.name: Sicilian Defence: Heidenfeld Variation
1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Na.strategy: A way to develop the queenside knight although c3 is occupied: from the rim it heads for c4 or b5, where it presses on d6 and supports e5. The knight starts far from the centre and the plan is slow, so Black gets time to attack the pawn centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.d4.strategy: Builds the pawn centre now that the knight guards it: d4 is attacked twice and defended three times, so ...cxd4 just lets White recapture with the c-pawn and keep a broad centre. White plays for space and quick development, and Black has to undermine e5 and d4 with pieces.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bc.strategy: Withdraws the knight from the bishop's attack and hits the bishop in the same move, so Black keeps the knight and wins a tempo. The knight is less active on b6 than on d5, but it guards the c4 square.

Supports the knight with a pawn. If White trades on d5 the recapture doubles Black's d-pawns and gives up the blockading knight, and the c8-bishop stays shut in, so Black gets a solid but passive game in which White's e5 pawn keeps its space advantage.
Hangs the knight: the pawn on d6 blocks the queen's protection of d5, so Bxd5 wins a piece outright.

1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bc.name: Sicilian Defence: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
1.e4 c5 2.c3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bc.strategy: Retreats the bishop but keeps it on the diagonal that points at f7 and at the d5 square. The bishop is away from the centre and can be harassed, so White trades a little time for lasting pressure against Black's kingside.

Retreats to a modest square, out of reach of any pawn push that would gain a tempo on it. Safe but passive: the bishop gives up the diagonal to f7 and has cost White two moves, so Black gets time to take space and develop freely.

Puts the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, but it blocks the d-pawn and can be hit at once by ...c4, which gains space with a tempo. After the retreat to c2 or e2 White has little to show for the detour, and Black has the space.

Hits the bishop with a pawn and takes space at once. Bxc4 loses the bishop for a pawn to ...Nxc4, so the bishop has to retreat. Black takes the d3 square from White, but the pawn needs the knight's support and no longer controls d4.

Challenges the e5 pawn directly: with the knight on c6 it is attacked twice and guarded only by the f3 knight, so White must trade or defend at once. Black gets a freer game than with ...c4, while White's bishop keeps its diagonal towards f7.

Blocks the bishop's diagonal at e6, covering d5 and shielding f7, and closes the e5 pawn in. Solid, but it shuts the c8-bishop behind its own pawn and leaves the e5 pawn as a cramping wedge, so Black has to find play against it with pieces.
